title: Control flow and traceable state

objectives.text: Apply a stated rejection policy before changing an accepted total.
Trace a loop and verify its invariant on each processed prefix, including empty input.
Track and flush maximal equal-character runs, including the final run, without replacing adjacency by global frequency.

blocks.markdown: A loop applies updates in order. If an invalid record changes the total before rejection, the program has already broken its policy. In this lesson supplied quantities are integers; positive values are accepted and nonpositive values are rejected. This is a synthetic exercise, not a universal policy for cancellation or signed-position events.

blocks.source:
quantities = [3, 0, 2, -1, 5]
accepted_total = 0
rejected_count = 0
for quantity in quantities:
    if quantity <= 0:
        rejected_count += 1
        continue
    accepted_total += quantity
print(accepted_total)
print(rejected_count)
blocks.caption: Expected output: 10, then 2. continue skips the rest of the current iteration, not the whole loop.

blocks.title: Inspect the state after each record

steps.text: After 0: total 3, rejects 1. The update is skipped.
After -1: total 5, rejects 2. The earlier total is unchanged.

blocks.markdown: The invariant is a claim that holds before the first update and after every processed record: accepted_total is the sum of positive quantities seen so far; rejected_count counts nonpositive quantities seen so far. Moving the total update before rejection would violate that claim for -1. continue does not undo earlier assignments.

Empty input has total 0 and rejects 0 because the accumulators are initialised before the loop. This code assumes integer inputs. Boundary validation still needs type checks: text and missing values are not automatically zero, and Python booleans need a deliberate policy if integer quantities exclude them.

A correct total for accepted records can still be incomplete. Report rejection counts and decide whether partial acceptance is allowed. A production boundary may instead reject the whole batch. This lesson has no external writes or trading effects.

Transfer to event state: keep a signed balance and the lowest balance seen, initially 0. Each event has a kind and an optional amount. Deposit D adds its amount. Withdrawal W first computes a candidate balance and accepts it only if it is at least minus the credit limit. Fee F subtracts 1 only while the balance is negative, and this fee is allowed to breach the withdrawal limit. Thus balance>=-limit is NOT a universal invariant. After every event, including a rejected withdrawal, update lowest=min(lowest,balance). A rejected withdrawal leaves the balance unchanged but still has an event index.

blocks.caption: Expected output: REJECT 3, then BALANCE 12, then MIN -8, with spaces between labels and values. Each pair in events contains kind and amount; F uses an unused 0. enumerate(...,start=1) gives a one-based event index. Input parsing is supplied separately in the practice starter.

blocks.markdown: Reference: [Python control flow](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html). All input is supplied locally; no market-data account, paid service or network action is needed.

Technical references: [Python control-flow tutorial](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html) for branches, loops and continue. The financial schemas, policies and synthetic cases in this lesson are declared teaching contracts, not claims about a particular venue or employer.

Pending run invariant

The input is one nonempty lowercase string, up to1000000characters. Maintain previous and count for the unfinished run at the end of the processed prefix. The token output contains exactly all completed earlier maximal runs in order. A matching character extends count. A different character completes the old run: append its character/count, then begin a new run of length1.

The final flush is necessary

When input ends, no different character arrives to flush the pending run. Append it explicitly after the loop. Each completed run becomes one token such as a3, with no internal space. For aaabbca, runs are a3,b2,c1,a1, each a glued character and decimal count. The final a is a new run, not combined with the initial a. Global frequency counting would lose this adjacency and order information. A one-character string has one final run and no change transition.

Parser and work boundaries

The public string has lowercase letters only, so the supplied whitespace-token parser preserves the complete string even when no final newline is present. Do not generalize that parser to strings containing spaces. One scan is O(len(s)), pending numeric/character state is fixed-size at these bounds, and stored output is O(number of runs). The iterator avoids copying a large suffix. The output is ONE joined string of run tokens such as a3 b2, with one space between tokens and no space inside a token. Return a one-element list containing this joined line: returning one list element per run would make the supplied main print separate lines and fail. No list brackets or colon separators are printed. Test constant, alternating, singleton and no-newline inputs.

blocks.source:
def run_lengths(s):
    characters = iter(s)
    previous = next(characters)
    count = 1
    tokens = []
    for character in characters:
        if character == previous:
            count += 1
        else:
            tokens.append(previous + str(count))
            (previous, count) = (character, 1)
    tokens.append(previous + str(count))
    return [' '.join(tokens)]

print(*run_lengths('aaabbca'))
print(*run_lengths('z'))
blocks.caption:
Expected stdout:
a3 b2 c1 a1
z1

summary: Check before updating. continue skips the rest of one iteration. Use a prefix invariant and explicit empty-input/rejection policy to make loop state inspectable. Practice transfer: maximal character runs.
